newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin plans to sober up Russian vodka market.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin plans to sober up Russian vodka market.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin plans to clamp strict control on production and sale of alcohol, squeezing the juice from what could be the Russian government's biggest source of roubles.
Yeltsin's press service said on Thursday he will sign a decree soon to enforce payment of duties and taxes by distillers, importers and retailers.

Every bottle of spirits is supposed to yield the treasury an 85 percent excise tax, 20 percent value-added tax and several additional taxes. Smugglers, moonshiners and bootleggers are estimated to be cheating the state of about two trillion roubles ($350 million) a month.

Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais told reporters the crackdown was decided by a special commission set up to deal with tax evasion and huge delays in the government's payment of wages and pensions.
Yeltsin chaired the meeting on his fourth day back in the Kremlin after months of absence due to heart problems.
Although Chubais spoke of restoring a state monopoly he also made clear the government did not plan a return to Soviet-era national ownership of distilleries and liquor shops.
The new order will be based on tight controls from the gates of Russia's approximately 700 distillers and strict licensing rules for producers, sellers and importers, Chubais said.
Russian vodka producers hailed the long-awaited move and said they hoped it would help legitimate producers and the state to cash in on Russia's traditional strong drink.
"The state will get additional revenues, the overall quality will rise. Fewer people will get poisoned with bad vodka," said Vladimir Yarmosh of Spirtprom (former Rosalco) producers' association.

Yarmosh said he expected the state to receive 10 or 12 percent of all budget revenues from vodka production and sales. In Soviet times, as well as before the revolution, the state used to earn up to one-third of its overall income from these sources.
This share has slumped dramatically to only two percent over the past decade, Yarmosh said.

He said output by legitimate producers could rise to two billion litres a year from less than a billion at the moment, or roughly a third of the industry's overall capacity, pushing up the price of vodka as well.

"Vodka is not milk but their prices are now similar in Russia. Prices should go up, it is in our interests," Yarmosh said. Producers said the industry was able to produce up to 2.7 to three billion litres of vodka a year.
Local moonshine and cheap imports from neighbouring Belarus and Ukraine had dealt a heavy blow to Russia's legal distilleries, driving many to the brink of collapse and cutting output at many others.
Chubais said the whole scheme of vodka imports from Belarus and Ukraine, which used to enjoy duty-free trade with Russia, would be reviewed.
Experts have estimated average annual imports of vodka and ethanol at 1.27 billion litres.

Yeltsin's decision is the latest in a series of efforts by the Russian government to sober up the national vodka industry that have included tightening up licensing and customs regulations and the recent introduction of import quotas.

Earlier this year the government announced 1997 import quotas of 100 million litres of strong liquors and 10 million litres of ethanol. The drastic import quotas are effective from January 1, 1997 and are aimed at protecting domestic producers.
